extracted.intended_audience: general educated public and practitioners (miners/geologists) interested in diamond mining and regional geology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on recognizing diamond-bearing gravels and primary beds, the geological reasoning about the origin of Brazilian diamonds, and the practical manual methods (washing, damming, probing) used to extract them in the Diamantina region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance of diamond-bearing cascalhos
rubrics_metrics.description: At first sight, they resemble the gravels of our rivers. They are formed of rounded pebbles of various colors, and are composed of numerous species of minerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These cascalhos (river gravels) have a peculiar appearance that never deceives the experienced miner; they commonly contain many mineral species and are the principal beds worked for diamonds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satellites (indicator minerals) of the diamond
rubrics_metrics.description: Quartz, the oxides of titanium, titanic iron, tourmalines, phosphates, fibrolite, octahedric oligist iron, and magnetite are the true satellites of the diamond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These minerals are 'sure to be found with it at Diamantina' and their constant association justifies believing the primitive bed of these minerals includes that of the diamond. Use presence of these minerals as a field indicator for diamond-bearing deposits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rounded/worn specimens indicate transport (alluvial origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: They have been brought down by the waters and worn round by friction. Fragments of diamond are found from which every trace of crystallization has disappeared, and which are as round as marbles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If diamonds and associated minerals are abraded, with wrinkled or smoothed faces, this indicates prolonged fluvial transport; thus rounded crystals point to alluvial (transported) origin rather than in-place crystallization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of 'caldeiroes' (giant pots) indicates locally richer sands
rubrics_metrics.description: These circular holes — the 'giants' pots,' the caldeiroes of the diamond-hunters — have sands that are naturally richer than the other sands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lighter elements are carried away from these holes by water and fragile substances ground to powder, concentrating diamonds. Discovery of a caldeiroe can yield very high immediate returns (examples: single caldeiroe furnishing nearly 8,000 carats) but such finds are rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical distribution as an indicator of source
rubrics_metrics.description: In the basin of the Jequitinhonha nearly all the water-courses are or have been diamond-bearing from their sources to their mouths; in basins of the Rio das Velhas and Rio Doce, streams cease to yield diamonds a short distance from their source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mapping which streams yield diamonds and the directions they depart from helps locate the source zone; presence of rich streams radiating from a zone suggests the primitive beds lie in that zone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association with gold and changing proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: In these streams, the diamond is always accompanied by gold in flakes or in little nuggets; while the diamond prevails in the center of the diamond-yielding region, as one moves toward the east the proportions are reversed: gold becomes more abundant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relative proportions of gold and diamond in sands as a spatial indicator of proximity to the diamond center; increasing gold proportion toward certain directions suggests changing provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field washing procedure (hods/troughs and bowls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sands are placed in portions of 200–250 pounds in a kind of hod or rectangular trough beside a trough of water; clay and fine sands are carried away, larger pieces picked away; final washing is done in bowls a little deeper and more conical than those used by gold-washers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First stage: coarse separation in hods with running water; secondary stage: bowl whirling to classify by density. The diamond is usually found in the upper two-thirds of the remaining mass; specific manual manipulations (whirling, shaking, stirring by hand) classify materials by density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density behavior during bowl washing (where diamonds settle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The diamond has a density about three and a half times that of water, more considerable than quartz and tourmaline but less than oxides of iron and titanium; it settles in the middle layers during washing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Washer recognizes the level by skill, removes upper particles, then tips bowl to let a thin film of water run off; the glittering crystals in the middle layers are picked out. Understand relative densities of companion minerals to target the correct layer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for vigilance and anti-fraud supervision during washing
rubrics_metrics.description: The vigilance of the overseers must be redoubled at this stage, particularly when slaves are employed; there are many artifices employed to steal diamonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: under old regulations fraud frequently took half the diamonds in the gravels; freer works have diminished fraud. Supervisors must be watchful during the crucial middle-layer extraction step.

rubrics_metrics.name: River-damming and flume method for working river beds
rubrics_metrics.description: The river is dammed and a flume of planks carries the water past the work area; pumps worked by water-wheels remove standing and infiltrating water while the intervening space is left free of running water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method permits working river channels that cannot be laterally sluiced; but it must be done quickly because sudden storms/freshets can destroy dams, wheels, and viaducts — occurring often (about half the time per the author). High risk of repetitive loss; timing in dry season (May–October) recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual excavation and transport techniques in trenches
rubrics_metrics.description: Only picks, shovels, levers to raise the rocks, and laborers who carry on their heads large wooden troughs are employed; no machines or inclined planes are commonly used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect deep, sinuous excavations where laborers work in gangs; primitive ladders and manual hauling are the norm despite available hydraulic power; logistical limits affect scale of operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probing to detect underlying cascalho and risk of exhausted deposits
rubrics_metrics.description: Overseers probe the sand with long iron rods; a peculiar sound familiar to all miners reveals the existence of diamond-bearing cascalho; disappointment occurs when the probe strikes rock without meeting diamonds because earlier miners removed them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic probing is a field diagnostic but subject to false negatives where previous mining removed deposits. Consider historical exploitation when evaluating negative probes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of primary/in-place (rock) deposits vs alluvial
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of the diamond in place in sandstones with green mica and in clay-beds shows diamonds can occur in the original strata; in primitive beds accompanying minerals appear in perfect crystals without trace of wearing, and diamonds there also show unmodified angles and faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If diamonds and their satellites occur as unabraded perfect crystals in rock/clay beds, interpret as primary/in-situ deposit rather than transported. This shifts exploration strategy from alluvial prospecting to bedrock investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using satellite mineralogy and stratigraphic position to infer origin/age
rubrics_metrics.description: The formations containing diamonds are intercalated with micaceous quartzites and compared with other Sao Francisco Valley strata; despite absence of fossils, correlation permits assigning them as far back as the Silurian period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine mineral assemblage (satellites) and regional stratigraphic correlations to infer the geological age and original setting of diamond-bearing formations — useful for exploration targeting and for hypotheses on genesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of crystal condition to distinguish transport/metamorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Crystals found rolled and rounded in river-sands present a different aspect from those in clays/primitive beds, which appear in perfect crystals without a trace of wearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the degree of crystal abrasion (rounded vs intact) of both diamonds and indicator minerals to evaluate whether deposits are reworked alluvium or preserved primary beds; consider possible metamorphic transformations of host formations when interpreting findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses on diamond formation mechanisms based on associations
rubrics_metrics.description: The constant association of diamonds with iron/titanium oxides and observations of synthetic experiments suggest diamonds may have been brought up as chlorides and fluorides and crystallized from a volatile compound under heat and pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is explicitly presented as a hypothesis (not resolved); use analogies with volcanic processes and laboratory synthesis (Daubree) to guide further research but treat as provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating production and valuing finds (practical expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brazilian production historically: e.g., between 1772 and 1793 the royal treasurer received 877,717 carats (~38,000 carats/year); 1880 production ~16 kg (~80,000 carats). Brazilian diamonds are generally small but noted for marked superiority in luster and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic expectations: large exceptional finds (e.g., Star of the South ~254.5 carats rough) are rare; regular mining yields are modest; compare with other regions (Cape mines produced ~2,000,000 carats in same period) when assessing economic potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational caution: extreme rarity of diamonds in primitive beds
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardly one diamond exists to a million crystals of oligist iron; more than thirty thousand pounds of clay have furnished only ten little diamonds weighing about a carat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume easy recovery in primary beds despite indicator minerals; expect extremely low concentration and that detection of individual diamonds in massive sterile matrices is improbable without intensive processing.
